authorial_core.interpreted_intent: The current reference points to the palace/court topic; this fresh independent image realizes royal court life. A random draw selected a court-musician rehearsal from three independently invented whole scenes. The chamber, musical role, two waiting courtiers, period palette, hands and dress are replaceable authorial staging, not requester definitions or claimed reference biography. The viewer should feel the threshold between solitary preparation and a formal performance, with subtle personal appeal carried by face, light and composed attention. A ceremonial throne portrait was considered as a static alternative; the music doorway relationship offers a more legible reason for the turn while remaining close to the court direction at creativity 1. Reference use is face/hair appearance guidance only, with no asserted identity or inferred age.
authorial_core.subject: A woman of the court, independently realized as a court musician.
authorial_core.setting: A fictional late-eighteenth-century European royal music salon.
authorial_core.event: A moment during a palace occasion, independently staged as an interrupted harpsichord rehearsal.
visual_priorities: The reference-guided woman remains the dominant presence as her attention turns from the instrument toward the waiting doorway.
Her two connected forearms, key contact and page contact can be understood in the same view.
The courtiers face the instrument through the open palace doorway, giving the turn an observable social cause.
Window light connects facial presence, pale silk and the worn formal salon without overwhelming the musical relationship.
authorial_core.baseline_prompt_en: A cinematic photographic scene of European royal court life, set during a palace occasion. A woman of the court sits at an open harpsichord in a late-eighteenth-century royal music salon, interrupted between rehearsal and the arrival of her audience. Use the supplied reference photograph as face-and-hair appearance guidance for this woman: a softly rounded oval face, dark brown eyes, a small straight nose, softly full pink lips, and a dark chin-length bob with light separated fringe. Her pale blue silk court gown has a fitted square-neck bodice, gently structured sleeves and a wide skirt settling over the upholstered bench. She turns her face toward the open gilded doorway, her lips faintly parted with alert composure; the private concentration of practice is becoming a public performance. Her right forearm leads visibly from her sleeve to a relaxed right hand resting on the keyboard, one fingertip pressing a single ivory key. Her left forearm reaches easily to the open score on the music desk, her left fingertips holding its lower outer corner flat. The wrists and page contact remain visible together. Both feet are supported beneath her settled seated posture. Beyond the doorway, two distant courtiers in formal dress have paused facing the instrument, their waiting attention explaining her turn. The harpsichord keyboard occupies the lower foreground; its music desk and the woman form the central triangle, with the doorway deeper at frame right. Tall palace windows at frame left give her face soft afternoon light and a restrained warm sheen along the silk neckline; worn gilding, patterned parquet and a single crimson chair supply the royal setting. Photograph from a three-quarter position beside the keyboard at seated eye height, a medium-wide view that includes the hands, music desk and doorway, natural facial texture, delicate film grain and quiet color separation. The woman remains the clear visual center; the audience is smaller and readable within the room rather than dissolved into abstraction.

intent_contract.text: The current reference points to the palace/court topic; this fresh independent image realizes royal court life. A random draw selected a court-musician rehearsal from three independently invented whole scenes. The chamber, musical role, two waiting courtiers, period palette, hands and dress are replaceable authorial staging, not requester definitions or claimed reference biography. The viewer should feel the threshold between solitary preparation and a formal performance, with subtle personal appeal carried by face, light and composed attention. A ceremonial throne portrait was considered as a static alternative; the music doorway relationship offers a more legible reason for the turn while remaining close to the court direction at creativity 1. Reference use is face/hair appearance guidance only, with no asserted identity or inferred age.

A cinematic photographic scene of European royal court life, set during a palace occasion. A woman of the court sits at an open harpsichord in a late-eighteenth-century royal music salon, interrupted between rehearsal and the arrival of her audience. Use the supplied reference photograph as face-and-hair appearance guidance for this woman: a softly rounded oval face, dark brown eyes, a small straight nose, softly full pink lips, and a dark chin-length bob with light separated fringe. Her pale blue silk court gown has a fitted square-neck bodice, gently structured sleeves and a wide skirt settling over the upholstered bench. She turns her face toward the open gilded doorway, her lips faintly parted with alert composure; the private concentration of practice is becoming a public performance. Her right forearm leads visibly from her sleeve to a relaxed right hand resting on the keyboard, one fingertip pressing a single ivory key. Her left forearm reaches easily to the open score on the music desk, her left fingertips holding its lower outer corner flat. The wrists and page contact remain visible together. Both feet are supported beneath her settled seated posture. Beyond the doorway, two distant courtiers in formal dress have paused facing the instrument, their waiting attention explaining her turn. The harpsichord keyboard occupies the lower foreground; its music desk and the woman form the central triangle, with the doorway deeper at frame right. Tall palace windows at frame left give her face soft afternoon light and a restrained warm sheen along the silk neckline; worn gilding, patterned parquet and a single crimson chair supply the royal setting. Photograph from a three-quarter position beside the keyboard at seated eye height, a medium-wide view that includes the hands, music desk and doorway, natural facial texture, delicate film grain and quiet color separation. The woman remains the clear visual center; the audience is smaller and readable within the room rather than dissolved into abstraction.
